title: Changing a nature grown evil
source_text: Καὶ ὁ μὲν Κέλσος φησὶ τὰ ἀκόλουθα ἑαυτῷ ἐπιφέρων ὅτι φύσιν ἀμεῖψαι τελέως παγχάλεπον. ἡμεῖς δὲ, μίαν φύσιν ἐπιστάμενοι πάσης λογικῆς ψυχῆς καὶ μηδεμίαν φάσκοντες πονηρὰν ὑπὸ τοῦ κτίσαντος τὰ ὅλα δεδημιουργῆσθαι, γεγονέναι (δὲ) πολλοὺς κακοὺς παρὰ τὰς ἀνατροφὰς καὶ τὰς διαστροφὰς καὶ τὰς περιηχήσεις, ὥστε καὶ φυσιωθῆναι ἔν τισι τὴν κακίαν, πειθόμεθα ὅτι τῷ θείῳ λόγῳ ἀμεῖψαι κακίαν φυσιώσασάν ἐστιν οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἀδύνατον ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐ πάνυ χαλεπὸν, ἐπὰν μόνον παραδέξηταί τις ὅτι πιστεύειν δεῖ ἑαυτὸν τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ καὶ πάντα πράττειν κατ᾿ ἀναφορὰν τοῦ ἀρέσκειν ἐκείνῳ· παρ᾿ ᾧ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν δὲ ἰῇ τιμῇ ἠμὲν κακὸς ἠδὲ καὶ ἐσθλός· οὐδὲ κάτθαν᾿ ὁμῶς ὅ τ᾿ ἀεργὸς ἀνὴρ ὅ τε πολλὰ ἐοργώς. εἰ δὲ καί τισι πάνυ χαλεπόν ἐστι τὸ μεταβάλλειν. τὴν αἰτίαν λεκτέον εἶναι περὶ τὴν συγκατάθεσιν αὐτῶν, ὀκνοῦσαν παραδέξασθαι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν εἶναι ἑκάστῳ δίκαιον κριτὴν περὶ πάντων τῶν ἐν τῷ βίῳ πεπραγμένων. μέγα γὰρ δύναται καὶ πρὸς τὰ δοκοῦντα εἶναι χαλεπώτατα καὶ, ἵνα καθ᾿ ὑπερβολὴν ὀνομάσω, ἐγγύς που ἀδύνατα προαίρεσις καὶ ἄσκησις. ἢ βουληθεῖσα ἀνθρωπίνη φύσις ἐπὶ κάλου βαίνειν, τεταμένου διὰ μέσου τοῦ θεάτρου ἐν μετεώρῳ, καὶ μετὰ τοῦ φέρειν τοσαῦτα καὶ τηλικαῦτα βάρη δεδύνηται τῇ ἀσκήσει καὶ τῇ προσοχῇ τὸ τοιοῦτο ποιῆσαι· βουληθεῖσα δὲ κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν βιῶσαι ἀδυνάτως ἔχει, κἂν ᾖ πρότερον φαυλοτάτη γεγενημένη; ἀλλ᾿ ὅρα μή ποτε ὁ τὰ τοιαῦτα λέγων τῇ δημιουργῷ τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου φύσει ἐγκαλεῖ μᾶλλον ἢ τῷ γεγενημένῳ. εἰ πρὸς μὲν τὰ οὕτω χαλεπὰ οὐδαμῶς ὄντα χρήσιμα πεποίηκε δυνατὴν τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσιν, ἀδύνατον δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἰδίαν μακαριότητα. ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὸ φύσιν γὰρ ἀμεῖψαι τελέως παγχάλεπον. ἑξῆς δέ φησιν ὅτι οἱ ἀναμάρτητοι βελτίους κοινωνοὶ βίου. μὴ σαφηνίσας, τίνας φησὶ τοὺς ἀναμαρτήτους, πότερον τοὺς ἀρχῆθεν ἢ τοὺς ἐκ μεταβολῆς. οἱ μὲν οὖν ἀρχῆθεν ἀδύνατοι, οἱ δ᾿ ἐκ μεταβολῆς σπανίως εἰσὶν εὑρισκόμενοι, οἵτινες ἐκ τοῦ προσεληλυθέναι λόγῳ σῴζοντι τοιοῦτοι γίνονται. οὐχὶ δὲ τοιοῦτοι ὄντες τῷ λόγῳ προσέρχονται· χωρὶς γὰρ λόγου καὶ ταῦτα τελείου ἀμήχανον ἀναμάρτητον γενέσθαι ἄνθρωπον.
pass_a_gloss: And Celsus says, bringing on (ἐπιφέρω) what follows (ἀκόλουθα) for himself, that 'to change (ἀμείβω) nature (φύσις) completely (τελέως) is very hard (παγχάλεπος).' But we, knowing (ἐπίσταμαι) one nature of every rational soul (λογικὴ ψυχή), and saying none was crafted (δημιουργέω) evil (πονηρός) by the one who created (κτίζω) the whole, but that many became bad (κακός) by reason of upbringings (ἀνατροφή), perversions (διαστροφή), and surrounding noises/talk (περιήχησις), so that in some evil (κακία) even became nature (φυσιόω), are persuaded (πείθομαι) that for the divine Word (θεῖος λόγος) to change evil that has become natural is not only not impossible (ἀδύνατος) but not very hard, if only one accepts (παραδέχομαι) that one must entrust (πιστεύω) oneself to the God over all and do (πράττω) all things with reference (ἀναφορά) to pleasing (ἀρέσκω) him; with whom it is not [so] 'in one honour (τιμή) both bad and noble (ἐσθλός); nor die alike (κάτθανε ὁμῶς) the idle (ἀεργός) man and the one who has done much' [Iliad 9.319-320]. If for some changing (μεταβάλλω) is very hard, the cause (αἰτία) must be said to be about their assent (συγκατάθεσις), hesitating (ὀκνέω) to accept that the God over all is to each a just judge (δίκαιος κριτής) about all things done in life. For choice (προαίρεσις) and training (ἄσκησις) are greatly able even toward things seeming hardest and, to name it by hyperbole (ὑπερβολή), nearly impossible. Or (ἤ, interrogative) has human nature, having willed (βούλομαι) to walk (βαίνω) on a rope (κάλως) stretched (τείνω) through the middle of the theatre (θέατρον) aloft (μετέωρος), and with carrying so many and such weights (βάρη), been able by training and attention (προσοχή) to do such a thing, but having willed to live according to virtue (ἀρετή) is unable, even if it had formerly become most base (φαυλότατος)? But see whether the one saying such things does not accuse (ἐγκαλέω) the creating (δημιουργός, adjective) nature of the rational living being (λογικὸν ζῷον) rather than what was made (γεγενημένον), if toward things so hard, being in no way useful (χρήσιμος), it has made human nature able (δυνατός), but unable toward its own blessedness (μακαριότης). But these things suffice toward 'for to change nature completely is very hard.' Next he says that 'the sinless (ἀναμάρτητοι) are better partners of life (κοινωνοὶ βίου),' not making clear (σαφηνίζω) whom he calls the sinless, whether those from the beginning (ἀρχῆθεν) or those from change (μεταβολή). Those from the beginning are impossible; those from change are found rarely (σπανίως), who become such from having come (προσέρχομαι) to the saving Word (λόγος σῴζων). They do not come to the Word being such; for without the Word, and that perfect (τέλειος), it is impossible (ἀμήχανος) for a man to become sinless.
pass_b_english: Celsus, drawing the consequence of his own view, says: “To change a nature completely is exceedingly hard.” But we know that every rational soul has one nature, and we hold that none was fashioned evil by the Creator of all things, but that many have become evil through their upbringing, through perversion and through the talk that surrounds them, so that in some people evil has even become second nature. And we are persuaded that for the divine Word to change an evil that has become second nature is not only not impossible but not even very hard, provided only that a person accepts that he must entrust himself to the God over all and do everything with a view to pleasing him. With him it is not true that “the base and the noble are held in one honour,” nor that “the idle man and the man who has done much die alike” (Homer, Iliad 9.319–320).

And if for some people change is very hard indeed, the cause must be said to lie in their assent, which shrinks from accepting that the God over all is a just judge of each person for all that he has done in life. For choice and training have great power even over things that seem hardest and, to speak in hyperbole, all but impossible. Or is it the case that human nature, when it has resolved to walk on a rope stretched high in the air across the middle of the theatre, and to carry so many and such heavy weights while doing it, has been able by training and attention to accomplish such a feat, but when it resolves to live by virtue it is incapable, even if it had formerly become utterly base? Consider whether the man who says such things is not finding fault with the nature that made the rational creature rather than with the creature that was made, if it has made human nature capable of things so hard and of no use whatever, but incapable of reaching its own blessedness. But this too is enough in answer to “For to change a nature completely is exceedingly hard.”

Next he says: “Those who are without sin are better companions in life.” He does not make clear whom he calls sinless, whether those who were so from the beginning or those who became so by a change. Those who were so from the beginning cannot exist; those who became so by a change are rarely found, and they become such through having come to the saving Word. They do not come to the Word already being such; for without the Word, and the perfect Word at that, it is impossible for a man to become sinless.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 69 (Koetschau 3.69); the local Perseus TEI (origen_celsum.xml) has the same wording. Celsus's words in direct quotation: 'To change a nature completely is exceedingly hard' (φύσιν ἀμεῖψαι τελέως παγχάλεπον; repeated with γάρ at the end of the second paragraph) and 'Those who are without sin are better companions in life' (οἱ ἀναμάρτητοι βελτίους κοινωνοὶ βίου). (δέ) is an editorial supplement. φυσιόω ('become nature') is rendered 'become second nature'. The Homer lines are Iliad 9.319-320 (Achilles' speech), which Origen quotes without naming and turns into a negation ('with him it is not ...'); the Homeric line has κάτθαν' ὁμῶς as the start of 9.320. Doubtful reading: τῇ δημιουργῷ τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου φύσει, with δημιουργός taken as a two-ending adjective ('the creating nature', i.e. what made the rational creature, God, who is the subject of πεποίηκε); some may prefer to emend to τῷ δημιουργῷ ('the Creator'); the sense is the same either way. χωρὶς λόγου καὶ ταῦτα τελείου: λόγος here is the saving Word just named, so capitalised; it could also be read 'without reason, and perfect reason at that'. No Scripture quotation; the idea that no one becomes sinless without the Word is not a quotation of a verse.
Checked the staged row against the Perseus TEI (origen_celsum.xml 3.69): complete, same wording
'their corruption' to 'through perversion' (διαστροφή, the Stoic term for the distortion of reason; kept parallel with ἀνατροφάς and περιηχήσεις)
'when it has willed ... when it wills' to 'when it has resolved ... when it resolves' (βουληθεῖσα, less stiff)
'so many heavy weights' to 'so many and such heavy weights' (τοσαῦτα καὶ τηλικαῦτα)
'even if it was formerly utterly base' to 'even if it had formerly become utterly base' (ᾖ ... γεγενημένη)
'But this is enough' to 'But this too is enough' (ἀρκεῖ καὶ ταῦτα)
Homer, Iliad 9.319-320 verified; Celsus's two sayings correctly quoted and attributed
